title: Electrical conductivity of a random nanowire network: comparison of two-dimensional and quasi-three-dimensional models
summary: It is shown that the widely used two-dimensional model of random networks of metallic nanowires or carbon nanotubes significantly overestimates the number of contacts between elements compared to real systems, which, within the mean-field approach, leads to overestimated estimates of electrical conductivity, especially when the contact resistances between conductors make the main contribution to the electrical conductivity of the system. In the case of a two-dimensional model, the electrical conductivity of the system depends quadratically on the number density of conductors, whereas in the case of a three-dimensional model this dependence is linear.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that 2D models of random metallic nanowire/carbon nanotube networks overestimate inter-element contacts compared to real 3D systems, leading to conductivity overestimation, especially when contact resistance dominates.
AI.motivation: To address the discrepancy between widely used 2D models of random conductive networks and real 3D systems, particularly regarding overestimation of inter-element contacts and resulting conductivity predictions.
AI.method: Comparison of 2D and 3D modeling approaches for random networks of metallic nanowires or carbon nanotubes, using mean-field analysis to examine contact statistics and their impact on electrical conductivity.
AI.result: 2D models significantly overestimate contact numbers between conductive elements compared to 3D reality, leading to overestimated conductivity predictions, especially when contact resistance dominates; conductivity scales quadratically with number density in 2D but linearly in 3D.
AI.conclusion: 3D modeling is essential for accurate prediction of electrical conductivity in random networks of metallic nanowires or carbon nanotubes, as 2D models produce systematically biased results due to overestimated contact statistics.

title: When low-loss paths make a binary neuron trainable: detecting algorithmic transitions with the connected ensemble
summary: We study the connected ensemble, a statistical-mechanics framework that characterizes the formation of low-loss paths in rugged landscapes. First introduced in a previous paper, this ensemble allows one to identify when a network can be trained on a simple task and which minima should be targeted during training. We apply this new framework to the symmetric binary perceptron model (SBP), and study how its typical {connected} minima behave. We show that {connected} minima exist only above a critical threshold $κ_{\rm connected}$, or equivalently below a critical constraint density $α_{\rm connected}$. This defines a parameter range in which training the network is easy, as local algorithms can efficiently access this connected manifold. We also highlight that these minima become increasingly robust and closer to one another as the task on which the network is trained becomes more difficult.

AI.tldr: The connected ensemble framework reveals that connected minima in the symmetric binary perceptron exist only above a critical threshold κ_connected, defining a parameter range where training is easy via local algorithms.
AI.motivation: To understand when neural networks can be trained on simple tasks and which minima should be targeted during training, using the connected ensemble framework to characterize low-loss path formation in rugged landscapes.
AI.method: Apply the connected ensemble framework to the symmetric binary perceptron model (SBP) to study the behavior of typical connected minima, analyzing their existence conditions and properties.
AI.result: Connected minima exist only above a critical threshold κ_connected (or below critical constraint density α_connected), defining a parameter range where training is easy. These minima become increasingly robust and closer together as task difficulty increases.
AI.conclusion: The connected ensemble provides a statistical-mechanics framework to identify when networks can be trained efficiently, with connected minima forming accessible manifolds that local algorithms can navigate, particularly in parameter ranges above κ_connected.

title: Practical Evaluation of Quantum Kernel Methods for Radar Micro-Doppler Classification on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) Hardware
summary: This paper examines the application of a Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM) for radarbased aerial target classification using micro-Doppler signatures. Classical features are extracted and reduced via Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to enable efficient quantum encoding. The reduced feature vectors are embedded into a quantum kernel-induced feature space using a fully entangled ZZFeatureMap and classified using a kernel based QSVM. Performance is first evaluated on a quantum simulator and subsequently validated on NISQ-era superconducting quantum hardware, specifically the IBM Torino (133-qubit) and IBM Fez (156-qubit) processors. Experimental results demonstrate that the QSVM achieves competitive classification performance relative to classical SVM baselines while operating on substantially reduced feature dimensionality. Hardware experiments reveal the impact of noise and decoherence and measurement shot count on quantum kernel estimation, and further show improved stability and fidelity on newer Heron r2 architecture. This study provides a systematic comparison between simulator-based and hardware-based QSVM implementations and highlights both the feasibility and current limitations of deploying quantum kernel methods for practical radar signal classification tasks.

AI.tldr: QSVM applied to radar target classification using micro-Doppler signatures achieves competitive performance vs classical SVM on reduced features, with systematic evaluation on quantum simulators and IBM quantum hardware revealing noise impacts and architecture improvements.
AI.motivation: To explore the application of quantum machine learning (specifically QSVM) for practical radar signal classification tasks, investigating whether quantum kernel methods can achieve competitive performance while operating on reduced feature dimensionality compared to classical approaches.
AI.method: Extract classical micro-Doppler features, reduce dimensionality via PCA, encode into quantum states using fully entangled ZZFeatureMap, implement kernel-based QSVM, evaluate on quantum simulator and validate on IBM quantum hardware (Torino 133-qubit and Fez 156-qubit processors).
AI.result: QSVM achieves competitive classification performance relative to classical SVM baselines despite using substantially reduced feature dimensionality. Hardware experiments reveal noise/decoherence impacts on kernel estimation, with improved stability/fidelity on newer Heron r2 architecture.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates feasibility of deploying quantum kernel methods for practical radar classification while highlighting current NISQ-era limitations, providing systematic comparison between simulator and hardware implementations and showing architecture-dependent performance improvements.

title: Probing Entanglement and Symmetries in Random States Using a Superconducting Quantum Processor
summary: Quantum many-body systems display an extraordinary degree of complexity, yet many of their features are universal: they depend not on microscopic details, but on a few fundamental physical aspects such as symmetries. A central challenge is to distill these universal characteristics from model-specific ones. Random quantum states sampled from a uniform distribution, the Haar measure, provide a powerful framework for capturing this typicality. Here, we experimentally study the entanglement and symmetries of random many-body quantum states generated by evolving simple product states under ergodic Floquet models. We find excellent agreement with the predictions from the Haar-random state ensemble. First, we measure the Rényi-2 entanglement entropy as a function of the subsystem size, observing the Page curve. Second, we probe the subsystem symmetries using entanglement asymmetry. Finally, we measure the moments of partially transposed reduced density matrices obtained by tracing out part of the system in the generated ensembles, thereby revealing distinct entanglement phases. Our results offer an experimental perspective on the typical entanglement and symmetries of many-body quantum systems.

AI.tldr: Experimental study of entanglement and symmetries in random quantum states generated via Floquet dynamics, showing agreement with Haar-random ensemble predictions including Page curve, entanglement asymmetry, and entanglement phases.
AI.motivation: To experimentally investigate universal entanglement and symmetry properties of many-body quantum systems by generating random states through ergodic dynamics and comparing with theoretical predictions from Haar-random ensembles.
AI.method: Generate random many-body quantum states by evolving simple product states under ergodic Floquet models. Measure: (1) Rényi-2 entanglement entropy vs subsystem size (Page curve), (2) subsystem symmetries via entanglement asymmetry, (3) moments of partially transposed reduced density matrices to reveal entanglement phases.
AI.result: Excellent agreement with Haar-random state ensemble predictions: observed Page curve for entanglement entropy, verified subsystem symmetry properties through entanglement asymmetry, and identified distinct entanglement phases via moments of partially transposed density matrices.
AI.conclusion: Experimental demonstration that Floquet-generated random states capture typical entanglement and symmetry properties predicted by Haar-random ensembles, providing experimental perspective on universal features of many-body quantum systems.

title: The Photonic Foundation of Temperature: Mechanisms of Thermal Equilibrium and Entropy Production
summary: I examine the physical foundations of temperature and thermal equilibrium by identifying photons as the fundamental agents that establish and maintain the characteristic energy scale $E_c = k_B T$ in ordinary matter. While classical thermodynamics successfully describes equilibrium phenomenologically, the realization of thermal distributions requires concrete microscopic mechanisms provided by quantum electrodynamics. We derive the Boltzmann distribution from a minimal differential scaling postulate and show that sustaining thermal equilibrium demands continuous photon exchange with average energy $\langle hν\rangle = 2.701\,E_c$, quantifying the energetic throughput necessary to counter radiative losses. Entropy production is shown to arise naturally from inelastic photon scattering that converts high-energy photons into many lower-energy quanta, thereby increasing accessible microstates and driving irreversible evolution toward equilibrium. We establish physical criteria distinguishing genuine thermal equilibrium from purely formal temperature assignments and demonstrate that the classical notion of an infinite thermal reservoir emerges as an effective idealization within a hierarchy of dynamically maintained photon baths. This photonic framework complements phenomenological thermodynamics by providing its microscopic foundation and clarifies the physical meaning of temperature as an emergent collective property of photon-mediated energy exchange.

AI.tldr: Photons are identified as fundamental agents establishing thermal equilibrium, with temperature emerging from photon-mediated energy exchange and entropy production arising from inelastic photon scattering.
AI.motivation: To provide microscopic foundations for temperature and thermal equilibrium by identifying concrete physical mechanisms beyond phenomenological thermodynamics, addressing how thermal distributions are actually realized and sustained in ordinary matter.
AI.method: Derives Boltzmann distribution from minimal differential scaling postulate; analyzes photon exchange requirements for sustaining equilibrium; examines entropy production through inelastic photon scattering; establishes physical criteria for genuine thermal equilibrium.
AI.result: Shows thermal equilibrium requires continuous photon exchange with average energy ⟨hν⟩ = 2.701Ec; demonstrates entropy production arises naturally from inelastic scattering converting high-energy photons to lower-energy quanta; establishes physical criteria distinguishing genuine equilibrium from formal temperature assignments.
AI.conclusion: Photons provide the microscopic foundation for thermodynamics, with temperature emerging as a collective property of photon-mediated energy exchange; classical infinite thermal reservoirs are effective idealizations within dynamically maintained photon baths.

title: Entanglement and discord classification via deep learning
summary: In this work, we propose a deep learning-based approach for quantum entanglement and discord classification using convolutional autoencoders. We train models to distinguish entangled from separable bipartite states for $d \times d$ systems with local dimension $d$ ranging from two to seven, which enables identification of bound and free entanglement. Through extensive numerical simulations across various quantum state families, we demonstrate that our model achieves high classification accuracy. Furthermore, we leverage the learned representations to generate samples of bound entangled states, the rarest form of entanglement and notoriously difficult to construct analytically. We separately train the same convolutional autoencoders architecture for detecting the presence of quantum discord and show that the model also exhibits high accuracy while requiring significantly less training time.

AI.tldr: Deep learning approach using convolutional autoencoders for classifying quantum entanglement and discord, achieving high accuracy and enabling generation of bound entangled states.
AI.motivation: To develop efficient methods for classifying quantum entanglement (including bound entanglement) and quantum discord, which are challenging to identify analytically, especially for higher-dimensional systems.
AI.method: Convolutional autoencoders trained on bipartite quantum states for d×d systems (d=2-7) to distinguish entangled from separable states and detect quantum discord presence.
AI.result: High classification accuracy across various quantum state families; successful generation of bound entangled states; significantly reduced training time for discord detection compared to entanglement classification.
AI.conclusion: Deep learning with convolutional autoencoders provides effective tools for quantum entanglement and discord classification, enabling identification of rare bound entanglement and offering computational advantages over analytical methods.

title: Some properties of coherent states with singular complex matrix argument
summary: In the paper our aim was to study the properties of a new version of coherent states whose argument is a linear combination of two special singular square 2 x 2 matrix, having a single nonzero element, equal to 1, and two labeling complex variables as developing coefficients. We have shown that this new version of coherent states satisfies all the conditions imposed on coherent states, both of pure, as well as the mixed (thermal) states characterized by the density operator. As applications, we examined the connection between these coherent states and the notions of qubits and von Neuman entropy.

AI.tldr: A new version of coherent states with arguments as linear combinations of singular 2x2 matrices and complex variables is introduced and shown to satisfy all coherent state conditions, with applications to qubits and von Neumann entropy.
AI.motivation: To study properties of a novel coherent state formulation using singular 2x2 matrices as arguments, extending coherent state theory to include matrix-valued arguments with applications in quantum information.
AI.method: Construct coherent states with arguments as linear combinations of two special singular 2x2 matrices (each having a single nonzero element equal to 1) and two complex labeling variables as coefficients, then verify satisfaction of coherent state conditions for both pure and mixed (thermal) states.
AI.result: The new coherent states satisfy all required conditions for coherent states, including those for pure states and mixed states characterized by density operators, enabling connections to quantum information concepts.
AI.conclusion: The developed coherent state framework successfully extends coherent state theory to include matrix arguments, providing mathematical tools for studying connections with qubits and von Neumann entropy in quantum information theory.

title: Three-dimensional squeezing of optically levitated nanospheres
summary: We propose a protocol to measure impulses beyond the standard quantum limit. The protocol reduces noise in all three spatial dimensions and consists of squeezing a mechanical system's state via a series of jumps in the frequency of the harmonic potential. We quantify how decoherence in a realistic system of an optically levitated, dielectric nanoparticle limits the ultimate sensitivity. We predict that $\sim$10 dB of squeezing is achievable with current technology, enabling quantum-enhanced detection of weak impulses.

AI.tldr: Protocol for measuring impulses beyond standard quantum limit using squeezing via frequency jumps in harmonic potential, achieving ~10 dB squeezing with current technology for quantum-enhanced detection.
AI.motivation: To overcome the standard quantum limit in impulse measurement by developing a protocol that reduces noise in all three spatial dimensions, enabling quantum-enhanced detection of weak impulses.
AI.method: Squeezing a mechanical system's state through a series of jumps in the frequency of the harmonic potential, applied to an optically levitated dielectric nanoparticle system, with analysis of decoherence limitations.
AI.result: Prediction that ~10 dB of squeezing is achievable with current technology, enabling quantum-enhanced detection of weak impulses beyond the standard quantum limit.
AI.conclusion: The proposed protocol successfully enables measurement of impulses beyond the standard quantum limit through mechanical squeezing, with practical feasibility demonstrated for optically levitated nanoparticles.

title: Efficient learning of logical noise from syndrome data
summary: Characterizing errors in quantum circuits is essential for device calibration, yet detecting rare error events requires a large number of samples. This challenge is particularly severe in calibrating fault-tolerant, error-corrected circuits, where logical error probabilities are suppressed to higher order relative to physical noise and are therefore difficult to calibrate through direct logical measurements. Recently, Wagner et al. [PRL 130, 200601 (2023)] showed that, for phenomenological Pauli noise models, the logical channel can instead be inferred from syndrome measurement data generated during error correction. Here, we extend this framework to realistic circuit-level noise models. From a unified code-theoretic perspective and spacetime code formalism, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for learning the logical channel from syndrome data alone and explicitly characterize the learnable degrees of freedom of circuit-level Pauli faults. Using Fourier analysis and compressed sensing, we develop efficient estimators with provable guarantees on sample complexity and computational cost. We further present an end-to-end protocol and demonstrate its performance on several syndrome-extraction circuits, achieving orders-of-magnitude sample-complexity savings over direct logical benchmarking. Our results establish syndrome-based learning as a practical approach to characterizing the logical channel in fault-tolerant quantum devices.

AI.tldr: The paper extends syndrome-based learning of logical quantum channels from phenomenological to circuit-level noise models, enabling efficient characterization of fault-tolerant circuits without direct logical measurements.
AI.motivation: Characterizing logical errors in fault-tolerant quantum circuits is challenging due to suppressed logical error probabilities requiring large sample sizes. Direct logical benchmarking is inefficient, while existing syndrome-based methods only work for phenomenological noise models.
AI.method: Extends syndrome-based learning framework to circuit-level noise using unified code-theoretic perspective and spacetime code formalism. Derives conditions for learning logical channels from syndrome data alone, characterizes learnable degrees of freedom of circuit-level Pauli faults, and develops efficient estimators using Fourier analysis and compressed sensing with provable guarantees.
AI.result: Developed an end-to-end protocol demonstrating orders-of-magnitude sample-complexity savings over direct logical benchmarking on several syndrome-extraction circuits. Established practical syndrome-based learning for characterizing logical channels in fault-tolerant devices.
AI.conclusion: Syndrome-based learning provides a practical, efficient approach to characterizing logical channels in fault-tolerant quantum devices, overcoming limitations of direct logical benchmarking and extending applicability to realistic circuit-level noise models.

title: Local-oscillator-agnostic squeezing detection
summary: We address the problem of measuring nonclassicality in continuous-variable bosonic systems without having access to a known reference signal. To this end, we construct broader classes of criteria for nonclassicality which allow us to investigate quantum phenomena regardless of the quantumness of selected subsystems. Such witnesses are based on the notion of partial normal ordering. This approach is applied to balanced homodyne detection using arbitrary, potentially nonclassical local oscillator states, yet only revealing the probed signal's quantumness. Our framework is compared to standard techniques, and the robustness and advanced sensitivity of our approach is shown. Therefore, a widely applicable framework, well-suited for applications in quantum metrology and quantum information, is derived to assess the quantum features of a photonic system when a well-defined coherent laser as a reference state is not available in the physical domain under study.

AI.tldr: Framework for measuring nonclassicality in continuous-variable systems without requiring known reference signals, using partial normal ordering criteria applicable to arbitrary local oscillator states.
AI.motivation: Address the problem of measuring nonclassicality in continuous-variable bosonic systems when a known reference signal (like a coherent laser) is unavailable, which is common in practical quantum applications.
AI.method: Construct broader classes of nonclassicality criteria based on partial normal ordering, allowing investigation of quantum phenomena regardless of subsystem quantumness. Apply to balanced homodyne detection with arbitrary (potentially nonclassical) local oscillator states while only revealing the probed signal's quantumness.
AI.result: Framework shows robustness and advanced sensitivity compared to standard techniques, enabling assessment of quantum features when well-defined coherent laser references are unavailable.
AI.conclusion: Derived a widely applicable framework suitable for quantum metrology and quantum information applications that can assess photonic system quantum features without requiring coherent laser reference states.

title: Quantum bootstrap product codes
summary: Product constructions constitute a powerful method for generating quantum CSS codes, yielding celebrated examples such as toric codes and asymptotically good low-density parity check (LDPC) codes. Since a CSS code is fully described by a chain complex, existing product formalisms are predominantly homological, defined via the tensor product of the underlying chain complexes of input codes, thereby establishing a natural connection between quantum codes and topology. In this Letter, we introduce the \textit{quantum bootstrap product} (QBP), an approach that extends beyond this standard homological paradigm. Specifically, a QBP code is determined by solving a consistency condition termed the ``bootstrap equation''. We find that the QBP paradigm unifies a wide range of important codes, including general hypergraph product (HGP) codes of arbitrary dimensions and fracton codes typically represented by the X-cube code. Crucially, the solutions to the bootstrap equation yield chain complexes where the chain groups and associated boundary maps consist of multiple components. We term such structures \textit{fork complexes}. This structure elucidates the underlying topological structures of fracton codes, akin to foliated fracton order theories. Beyond conceptual insights, we demonstrate that the QBP paradigm can generate self-correcting quantum codes from input codes with constant energy barriers and surpass the code-rate upper bounds inherent to HGP codes. Our work thus substantially extends the scope of quantum product codes and provides a versatile framework for designing fault-tolerant quantum memories.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Quantum Bootstrap Product (QBP), a novel framework for constructing quantum CSS codes that extends beyond standard homological product methods, unifying various important codes including hypergraph product codes and fracton codes, while enabling improved code properties.
AI.motivation: Existing product constructions for quantum CSS codes are predominantly homological and based on tensor products of chain complexes. This approach has limitations and doesn't capture the full range of important quantum codes, particularly fracton codes. There's a need for a more general framework that can unify different code families and potentially yield better code properties.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Quantum Bootstrap Product (QBP) paradigm, where codes are determined by solving a "bootstrap equation" rather than through standard tensor products. This approach yields "fork complexes" - chain complexes where chain groups and boundary maps consist of multiple components. The framework extends beyond homological product methods and can generate codes from input codes with constant energy barriers.
AI.result: The QBP framework unifies various important code families including general hypergraph product codes of arbitrary dimensions and fracton codes (like X-cube codes). It generates fork complexes that elucidate the topological structures of fracton codes, similar to foliated fracton order theories. The approach can produce self-correcting quantum codes from input codes with constant energy barriers and surpasses code-rate upper bounds inherent to HGP codes.
AI.conclusion: The Quantum Bootstrap Product substantially extends the scope of quantum product codes, providing a versatile framework for designing fault-tolerant quantum memories that goes beyond traditional homological methods and captures a broader range of quantum code structures.

title: Manjushri: A Tool for Equivalence Checking of Quantum Circuits
summary: Verifying whether two quantum circuits are equivalent is a central challenge in the compilation and optimization of quantum programs. We introduce \textsc{Manjushri}, a new automated framework for scalable quantum-circuit equivalence checking. \textsc{Manjushri} uses local projections as discriminative circuit fingerprints, implemented with weighted binary decision diagrams (WBDDs), yielding a compact and efficient symbolic representation of quantum behavior. We present an extensive experimental evaluation that, for random 1D Clifford+$T$ circuits, explores the trade-off between \textsc{Manjushri} and \textsc{ECMC}, a tool for equivalence checking based on a much different approach. \textsc{Manjushri} is much faster up to depth 30 (with the crossover point varying from 39--49, depending on the number of qubits and whether the input circuits are equivalent or inequivalent): when inputs are equivalent, \textsc{Manjushri} is about 10$\times$ faster (or more); when inputs are inequivalent, \textsc{Manjushri} is about 8$\times$ faster (or more). For both kinds of equivalence-checking outcomes, \textsc{ECMC}'s success rate out to depth 50 is impressive on 32- and 64-qubit circuits: on such circuits, \textsc{ECMC} is almost uniformly successful. However, \textsc{ECMC} struggled on 128-qubit circuits for some depths. \textsc{Manjushri} is almost uniformly successful out to about depth 38, before tailing off to about 75\% at depth 50 (falling to 0\% at depth 48 for 128-qubit circuits that are equivalent). These results establish that \textsc{Manjushri} is a practical and scalable solution for large-scale quantum-circuit verification, and would be the preferred choice unless clients need to check equivalence of circuits of depth $>$38.

AI.tldr: Manjushri is a scalable quantum-circuit equivalence checking framework using local projections with WBDDs, outperforming ECMC for circuits up to depth ~38, with 8-10× speedup for both equivalent and inequivalent circuits.
AI.motivation: Quantum circuit equivalence checking is essential for compilation and optimization of quantum programs, but existing methods face scalability challenges with large circuits.
AI.method: Uses local projections as discriminative circuit fingerprints implemented with weighted binary decision diagrams (WBDDs) for compact symbolic representation of quantum behavior.
AI.result: Manjushri is 8-10× faster than ECMC up to depth 30, with crossover at depth 39-49. For equivalent circuits, it's 10×+ faster; for inequivalent, 8×+ faster. Manjushri succeeds uniformly to depth ~38, then declines to ~75% at depth 50, while ECMC struggles with 128-qubit circuits.
AI.conclusion: Manjushri is a practical, scalable solution for large-scale quantum-circuit verification, preferred for circuits up to depth ~38, establishing its effectiveness for quantum program compilation and optimization.

title: On the undecidability of quantum channel capacities
summary: An important distinction in our understanding of capacities of classical versus quantum channels is marked by the following question: is there an algorithm which can compute (or even efficiently compute) the capacity? While there is overwhelming evidence suggesting that quantum channel capacities may be uncomputable, a formal proof of any such statement is elusive. We initiate the study of the hardness of computing quantum channel capacities. We show that, for a general quantum channel, it is QMA-hard to compute its quantum capacity, and that the maximal-entanglement-assisted zero-error one-shot classical capacity is uncomputable.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that computing quantum channel capacities is computationally hard: quantum capacity is QMA-hard to compute, and maximal-entanglement-assisted zero-error one-shot classical capacity is uncomputable.
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental computational differences between classical and quantum channel capacities, specifically whether there exist algorithms to compute quantum channel capacities, given evidence suggesting they may be uncomputable.
AI.method: The authors initiate the study of hardness of computing quantum channel capacities through computational complexity analysis, showing reductions to known hard problems and proving uncomputability results.
AI.result: Two main results: (1) Computing the quantum capacity of a general quantum channel is QMA-hard (quantum analogue of NP-hard), and (2) The maximal-entanglement-assisted zero-error one-shot classical capacity is uncomputable.
AI.conclusion: Quantum channel capacities exhibit fundamental computational hardness properties, with quantum capacity being QMA-hard and certain entanglement-assisted capacities being uncomputable, highlighting significant computational barriers in quantum information theory.

title: Dicke States for Accelerated Two Two-Level Atoms
summary: We explore the formation of Dicke states. A system consisting of two two-level atoms located in the right Rindler wedge, has investigated to determine the conditions under which the superradiant or subradiant state can be formed. The dynamics of N two-level atoms forming symmetric state has also been analyzed and showed that the probability to excite any one atom of a collection of N atoms is related to the probability of exciting a single atom. We derive the analytical expression for the joint excitation probability which demonstrates the the interference effect. These findings provide new insights into the behavior of quantum systems in non-inertial frames and contribute to the broader understanding of relativistic quantum information theory.

AI.tldr: Analysis of Dicke state formation in relativistic quantum systems, showing superradiant/subradiant state conditions for atoms in Rindler wedge and relating N-atom excitation probabilities to single-atom probabilities.
AI.motivation: To understand the formation of Dicke states (superradiant and subradiant states) in relativistic quantum systems, specifically investigating quantum systems in non-inertial frames and contributing to relativistic quantum information theory.
AI.method: Studied a system of two two-level atoms in the right Rindler wedge to determine conditions for superradiant/subradiant state formation. Analyzed dynamics of N two-level atoms forming symmetric states. Derived analytical expressions for joint excitation probabilities showing interference effects.
AI.result: Found conditions for superradiant or subradiant state formation for two atoms in Rindler wedge. Showed that probability to excite any one atom in a collection of N atoms is related to single-atom excitation probability. Derived analytical expression for joint excitation probability demonstrating interference effects.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide new insights into quantum system behavior in non-inertial frames and contribute to the broader understanding of relativistic quantum information theory, particularly regarding Dicke state formation and excitation probabilities in relativistic contexts.

title: Structural Conditions for Native CCZ Magic-State Fountains in qLDPC Codes
summary:
Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes promise constant-rate, linear-distance families with bounded-weight checks, and recent work has realized transversal or constant-depth non-Clifford gates on various (often non-LDPC) codes. However, no explicit \emph{qubit} qLDPC family is known that simultaneously has constant rate, linear distance, bounded stabilizer weight, and a native \emph{magic-state fountain} that prepares many non-Clifford resource states in constant depth.
  We take a structural approach and identify coding-theoretic conditions under which a CSS qLDPC family necessarily supports a constant-depth $\CCZ$ magic-state fountain. The key ingredients are: (i) an algebraic notion of \emph{magic-friendly triples} of $X$-type logical operators, defined by pairwise orthogonality and a triple-overlap form controlling diagonal $\CCZ$ phases, and (ii) a 3-uniform hypergraph model of physical $\CCZ$ circuits combined with a packing lemma that turns large collections of such triples with bounded overlaps into bounded-degree hypergraphs.
  Our main theorem shows that if a CSS code family on $n$ qubits admits $Ω(n^{1+γ})$ magic-friendly triples whose supports have bounded per-qubit participation, then there exists a constant-depth circuit of physical $\CCZ$ gates implementing $Ω(n^γ)$ logical $\CCZ$ gates in parallel while preserving distance up to a constant factor. For asymptotically good qLDPC families such as quantum Tanner codes, this reduces the existence of a native $\CCZ$ magic-state fountain to a concrete combinatorial problem about counting and distributing magic-friendly triples in the logical $X$ space.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies coding-theoretic conditions for CSS qLDPC codes to support constant-depth CCZ magic-state fountains, reducing the problem to counting magic-friendly triples in the logical X space.
AI.motivation: No explicit qubit qLDPC family exists that simultaneously has constant rate, linear distance, bounded stabilizer weight, and a native magic-state fountain for preparing many non-Clifford resource states in constant depth.
AI.method: Introduces magic-friendly triples of X-type logical operators with pairwise orthogonality and triple-overlap form controlling diagonal CCZ phases, combined with a 3-uniform hypergraph model of physical CCZ circuits and a packing lemma to convert large collections of such triples into bounded-degree hypergraphs.
AI.result: Main theorem: If a CSS code family on n qubits admits Ω(n^{1+γ}) magic-friendly triples with bounded per-qubit participation, then there exists a constant-depth circuit of physical CCZ gates implementing Ω(n^γ) logical CCZ gates in parallel while preserving distance up to a constant factor.
AI.conclusion: For asymptotically good qLDPC families like quantum Tanner codes, the existence of a native CCZ magic-state fountain reduces to a concrete combinatorial problem about counting and distributing magic-friendly triples in the logical X space.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Sensing Enabled by Scrambling-Induced Genuine Multipartite Entanglement
summary: Quantum sensing leverages quantum resources to surpass the standard quantum limit, yet many existing protocols rely on the preparation of complex entangled states and Hamiltonian engineering, posing challenges for universality and scalability. Here, we report an experimental realization of a universal protocol, known as Butterfly Metrology, proposed in [arXiv:2411.12794], demonstrating a scrambling-based approach for quantum-enhanced sensing on a superconducting quantum processor. By exploiting many-body information scrambling, we observe quantum-enhanced sensitivity to an encoded phase beyond the standard quantum limit, with a scaling consistent with a factor-of-two of the Heisenberg limit for system sizes of up to 10 qubits. Importantly, we experimentally establish a connection between the enhanced sensitivity and the dynamics of the out-of-time-order correlator (OTOC), and show that the buildup of scrambling-induced genuine multipartite entanglement underlies the observed sensitivity enhancement. Our results demonstrate a scalable and practical approach for quantum-enhanced sensing in interacting many-body quantum systems.

AI.tldr: Experimental demonstration of Butterfly Metrology on superconducting quantum processor achieves quantum-enhanced sensing beyond standard quantum limit using many-body information scrambling, showing scaling approaching Heisenberg limit for up to 10 qubits.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum sensing protocols often require complex entangled state preparation and Hamiltonian engineering, limiting universality and scalability. The paper aims to demonstrate a more practical, scalable approach using scrambling-based metrology.
AI.method: Implementation of Butterfly Metrology protocol on superconducting quantum processor, exploiting many-body information scrambling. The approach connects enhanced sensitivity to out-of-time-order correlator (OTOC) dynamics and scrambling-induced genuine multipartite entanglement.
AI.result: Achieved quantum-enhanced sensitivity beyond standard quantum limit with scaling consistent with factor-of-two of Heisenberg limit for system sizes up to 10 qubits. Established experimental connection between enhanced sensitivity and OTOC dynamics, showing scrambling-induced genuine multipartite entanglement underlies sensitivity enhancement.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates a scalable and practical approach for quantum-enhanced sensing in interacting many-body quantum systems using scrambling-based metrology, offering advantages over protocols requiring complex entangled state preparation.

title: Analysis of self-thermalization dynamics in the Bose-Hubbard model by using the pseudoclassical approach
summary: We analyze the self-thermalization dynamics of the $M$-site Bose-Hubbard model in terms of the single-particle density matrix that is calculated by using the pseudoclassical approach. It is shown that a weak inter-particle interaction, which suffices to convert the integrable system of non-interacting bosons into a chaotic system, has a negligible effect on the thermal density matrix given by the Bose-Einstein distribution. This opens the door for equilibration where the two coupled Bose-Hubbard systems, which are initially in different thermal states, relax to the same thermal state. When we couple these two subsystems by using a lattice of the length $L\ll M$, we numerically calculate the quasi-stationary current of Bose particles across the lattice and show that its magnitude is consistent with the solution of the master equation for the boundary driven $L$-site Bose-Hubbard model.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes self-thermalization in the M-site Bose-Hubbard model using pseudoclassical approach, showing weak interactions induce chaos but negligibly affect thermal density matrix, enabling equilibration between coupled subsystems and quasi-stationary current calculations.
AI.motivation: To understand how weak inter-particle interactions affect thermalization dynamics in Bose-Hubbard systems, particularly how integrable systems become chaotic and how this enables equilibration between coupled subsystems initially in different thermal states.
AI.method: Uses pseudoclassical approach to calculate single-particle density matrix for M-site Bose-Hubbard model. Numerical calculations of quasi-stationary current across lattice when coupling two subsystems via lattice of length L ≪ M. Compares results with master equation solution for boundary-driven L-site Bose-Hubbard model.
AI.result: Weak inter-particle interaction suffices to convert integrable system of non-interacting bosons into chaotic system but has negligible effect on thermal density matrix given by Bose-Einstein distribution. This enables equilibration where two coupled Bose-Hubbard systems initially in different thermal states relax to same thermal state. Quasi-stationary current magnitude across lattice is consistent with master equation solution for boundary-driven L-site Bose-Hubbard model.
AI.conclusion: Weak interactions induce chaos in Bose-Hubbard systems without significantly altering thermal density matrices, facilitating thermalization and equilibration between coupled subsystems. The consistency between numerical current calculations and master equation solutions validates the approach for studying transport properties in these systems.

title: Towards Sample Efficient Entanglement Classification for 3 and 4 Qubit Systems: A Tailored CNN-BiLSTM Approach
summary: Accurate classification of multipartite entanglement in high-dimensional quantum systems is crucial for advancing quantum communication and information processing. However, conventional methods are resource-intensive, and even many machine-learning-based approaches necessitate large training datasets, creating a significant experimental bottleneck for data acquisition. To address this challenge, we propose a hybrid neural network architecture integrating Convolutional and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory networks (CNN-BiLSTM). This design leverages CNNs for local feature extraction and BiLSTMs for sequential dependency modeling, enabling robust feature learning from minimal training data. We investigate two fusion paradigms: Architecture 1 (flattening-based) and Architecture 2 (dimensionality-transforming). When trained on only 100 samples, Architecture 2 maintains classification accuracies exceeding 90% for both 3-qubit and 4-qubit systems, demonstrating rapid loss convergence within tens of epochs. Under full-data conditions (400 000 samples), both architectures achieve accuracies above 99.97%. Comparative benchmarks reveal that our CNN-BiLSTM models, especially Architecture 2, consistently outperform standalone CNNs, BiLSTMs, and MLPs in low-data regimes, albeit with increased training time. These results demonstrates that the tailored CNN-BiLSTM fusion significantly alleviates experimental data acquisition burden, offering a practical pathway toward scalable entanglement verification in complex quantum systems.

AI.tldr: Hybrid CNN-BiLSTM architecture achieves high accuracy in multipartite entanglement classification with minimal training data, reducing experimental data acquisition burden.
AI.motivation: Conventional methods for multipartite entanglement classification are resource-intensive, and even machine learning approaches require large training datasets, creating experimental bottlenecks for data acquisition in quantum systems.
AI.method: Proposed hybrid neural network architecture integrating Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for local feature extraction and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory networks (BiLSTMs) for sequential dependency modeling. Investigated two fusion paradigms: Architecture 1 (flattening-based) and Architecture 2 (dimensionality-transforming).
AI.result: With only 100 training samples, Architecture 2 maintains classification accuracies exceeding 90% for both 3-qubit and 4-qubit systems, with rapid loss convergence within tens of epochs. Under full-data conditions (400,000 samples), both architectures achieve accuracies above 99.97%. CNN-BiLSTM models, especially Architecture 2, outperform standalone CNNs, BiLSTMs, and MLPs in low-data regimes, though with increased training time.
AI.conclusion: The tailored CNN-BiLSTM fusion significantly alleviates experimental data acquisition burden, offering a practical pathway toward scalable entanglement verification in complex quantum systems.

title: Two-parameter bipartite entanglement measure
summary: Entanglement concurrence is an important bipartite entanglement measure that has found wide applications in quantum technologies. In this work, inspired by unified entropy, we introduce a two-parameter family of entanglement measures, referred to as the unified $(q,s)$-concurrence. Both the standard entanglement concurrence and the recently proposed $q$-concurrence emerge as special cases within this family. By combining the positive partial transposition and realignment criteria, we derive an analytical lower bound for this measure for arbitrary bipartite mixed states, revealing a connection to strong separability criteria. Explicit expressions are obtained for the unified $(q,s)$-concurrence in the cases of isotropic and Werner states under the constraint $q>1$ and $qs\geq 1$. Furthermore, we explore the monogamy properties of the unified $(q,s)$-concurrence for $q\geq 2$, $0\leq s\leq 1$ and $1\leq qs\leq 3$, in qubit systems. In addition, we derive an entanglement polygon inequality for the unified $(q,s)$-concurrence with $q\geq 1$ and $qs\geq 1$, which manifests the relationship among all the marginal entanglements in any multipartite qudit system.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a two-parameter family of entanglement measures called unified (q,s)-concurrence, which generalizes both standard concurrence and q-concurrence, and provides analytical bounds, explicit calculations for specific states, and explores monogamy properties.
AI.motivation: To develop a more comprehensive family of entanglement measures that unifies existing concurrence measures and provides a framework for analyzing bipartite entanglement with greater flexibility through two adjustable parameters.
AI.method: Introduces unified (q,s)-concurrence inspired by unified entropy; derives analytical lower bounds using PPT and realignment criteria; obtains explicit expressions for isotropic and Werner states; explores monogamy properties in qubit systems; derives entanglement polygon inequality for multipartite systems.
AI.result: Successfully created a two-parameter family of entanglement measures that generalizes existing concurrence measures; derived analytical lower bounds connecting to strong separability criteria; obtained explicit formulas for specific state classes; established monogamy properties and entanglement polygon inequality.
AI.conclusion: The unified (q,s)-concurrence provides a flexible framework for quantifying bipartite entanglement that encompasses existing measures, offers analytical tools for bounding entanglement, and reveals structural relationships in multipartite systems through monogamy and polygon inequalities.

title: Multipartite entanglement measures based on the thermodynamic framework
summary: In this work, we introduce a unified method to characterize and measure multipartite entanglement using the framework of thermodynamics. A family of the new entanglement measures is proposed: \textit{ergotropic-gap concentratable entanglement}. Furthermore, we establish that ergotropic-gap concentratable entanglement constitutes a well-defined entanglement measure within a specific parameter regime, satisfying key properties including continuity, majorization monotonicity and monogamy. We demonstrate the utility of this measure by showing it effectively distinguishes between multi-qubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states and W states. It also proves effective in detecting entanglement in specific classes of four-partite star quantum network states.

AI.tldr: Proposes ergotropic-gap concentratable entanglement as a new family of multipartite entanglement measures based on thermodynamic framework, demonstrating utility for distinguishing GHZ vs W states and detecting entanglement in star network states.
AI.motivation: To develop a unified thermodynamic framework for characterizing and measuring multipartite entanglement, addressing the need for effective entanglement measures that can distinguish between different types of multipartite entangled states and work in quantum network scenarios.
AI.method: Introduces ergotropic-gap concentratable entanglement measures using thermodynamic principles, establishes mathematical properties within specific parameter regimes, and applies the measures to analyze multi-qubit GHZ states, W states, and four-partite star quantum network states.
AI.result: The ergotropic-gap concentratable entanglement constitutes a well-defined entanglement measure satisfying continuity, majorization monotonicity, and monogamy properties. It effectively distinguishes between GHZ and W states and detects entanglement in four-partite star quantum network states.
AI.conclusion: The thermodynamic framework provides a unified approach to multipartite entanglement characterization, with ergotropic-gap concentratable entanglement serving as a practical measure with proven mathematical properties and demonstrated utility for important classes of quantum states.

title: Unconventional Distance Scaling of Casimir-Polder Force between Atomic Arrays
summary: Conventionally, dispersion forces mediated by quantum vacuum fluctuations are known to exhibit universal distance scalings, with retardation typically leading to a faster decay of the interaction. Here, we show that this expectation fails for intrinsically discrete systems. Using the microscopic scattering approach, we study the Casimir-Polder interaction between two atomic arrays, and uncover an unconventional distance scaling in which the force crosses over from a faster decay at short separations to a slower decay in the retarded regime. This behavior originates from the discrete lattice structure and can be consistently understood within the scattering picture. Extending our analysis to Rydberg atomic arrays, we predict an even stronger deviation from conventional scaling and propose an experimentally feasible scheme for direct measurement. Our results provide a new platform for exploring dispersion forces beyond the continuum limit.

AI.tldr: Casimir-Polder forces between atomic arrays exhibit unconventional distance scaling: faster decay at short separations, slower decay in retarded regime due to discrete lattice structure, with stronger deviations in Rydberg arrays.
AI.motivation: Conventional dispersion forces mediated by quantum vacuum fluctuations exhibit universal distance scalings with retardation typically leading to faster decay. This work challenges the expectation that this universal behavior holds for intrinsically discrete systems.
AI.method: Using the microscopic scattering approach to study Casimir-Polder interaction between two atomic arrays. Analysis extended to Rydberg atomic arrays with proposed experimental measurement scheme.
AI.result: Uncovered unconventional distance scaling where the force crosses over from faster decay at short separations to slower decay in the retarded regime. This behavior originates from discrete lattice structure and can be understood within scattering picture. Rydberg arrays show even stronger deviation from conventional scaling.
AI.conclusion: Results provide a new platform for exploring dispersion forces beyond the continuum limit, demonstrating that discrete systems can exhibit fundamentally different scaling behavior than continuum expectations.

title: Orders of magnitude runtime reduction in quantum error mitigation
summary: Quantum error mitigation (QEM) infers noiseless expectation values by combining outcomes from intentionally modified, noisy variants of a target quantum circuit. Unlike quantum error correction, QEM requires no additional hardware resources and is therefore routinely employed in experiments on contemporary quantum processors. A central limitation of QEM is its substantial sampling overhead, which necessitates long execution times where device noise may drift, potentially compromising the reliability of standard mitigation protocols. QEM strategies based on agnostic noise amplification (ANA) are intrinsically resilient to such noise variations, but their sampling cost remains a major practical bottleneck. Here we introduce a mitigation framework that combines virtual noise scaling with a layered mitigation architecture, yielding orders of magnitude reduction in runtime overhead compared to conventional zero-noise extrapolation post-processing. The proposed approach is compatible with dynamic circuits and can be seamlessly integrated with error detection and quantum error correction schemes. In addition, it naturally extends to ANA-based mitigation of mid-circuit measurements and preparation errors. We validate our post-processing approach by applying it to previously reported experimental data, where we observe a substantial improvement in mitigation efficiency and accuracy.

AI.tldr: A quantum error mitigation framework combining virtual noise scaling with layered architecture achieves orders of magnitude runtime reduction compared to conventional zero-noise extrapolation, while maintaining resilience to noise variations and compatibility with dynamic circuits and error correction schemes.
AI.motivation: Quantum error mitigation (QEM) faces substantial sampling overhead leading to long execution times where device noise may drift, compromising reliability of standard protocols. While agnostic noise amplification (ANA) strategies are resilient to noise variations, their sampling cost remains a major practical bottleneck.
AI.method: Combines virtual noise scaling with a layered mitigation architecture, enabling orders of magnitude reduction in runtime overhead compared to conventional zero-noise extrapolation post-processing. The approach is compatible with dynamic circuits and can be integrated with error detection and quantum error correction schemes, and naturally extends to ANA-based mitigation of mid-circuit measurements and preparation errors.
AI.result: Validated by applying to previously reported experimental data, showing substantial improvement in mitigation efficiency and accuracy. The framework achieves orders of magnitude reduction in runtime overhead while maintaining resilience to noise variations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed mitigation framework significantly reduces the practical bottleneck of sampling overhead in quantum error mitigation while maintaining compatibility with existing quantum computing architectures and error handling schemes, representing a substantial advancement in practical quantum error mitigation techniques.

title: Scattering of Squeezed Light by a Dielectric Slab
summary: We develop a quantum theory for the scattering of squeezed coherent light by a dissipative dielectric slab. Using the Green-function quantization approach, we derive the transformation of the field quadratures and show how dispersion, absorption, and multiple reflections distort the incident squeezing. We find that the slab can selectively attenuate or amplify quadrature noise depending on the slab parameters and provide expressions for the output power spectra.

AI.tldr: Quantum theory for scattering of squeezed coherent light by dissipative dielectric slab using Green-function quantization, showing how dispersion, absorption, and multiple reflections distort squeezing and selectively affect quadrature noise.
AI.motivation: To develop a quantum theory for understanding how squeezed coherent light interacts with dissipative dielectric slabs, particularly how dispersion, absorption, and multiple reflections affect quantum squeezing properties.
AI.method: Uses Green-function quantization approach to derive transformation of field quadratures for squeezed coherent light scattering through dissipative dielectric slab.
AI.result: Slab can selectively attenuate or amplify quadrature noise depending on slab parameters; derived expressions for output power spectra showing distortion of incident squeezing.
AI.conclusion: Developed comprehensive quantum theory showing how dielectric slab properties (dispersion, absorption, multiple reflections) modify squeezed light, enabling selective quadrature noise manipulation.

title: Steady-State Emission of Quantum-Correlated Light in the Telecom Band from a Single Atom
summary: We propose and investigate a scheme for the steady-state emission of quantum-correlated, telecom-band light from a single multilevel atom. By appropriately tuning the frequency of a pair of lasers, a two-photon transition is continually driven to an atomic excited state that emits photons at the desired wavelength. We show that resonantly coupling a cavity mode to the telecom transition can enhance the rate of emission while retaining the antibunched counting statistics that are characteristic of atomic light sources. We also explore coupling a second, independent cavity mode to the atom, which increases the telecom emission rate and introduces quantum correlations between the cavity modes. A model for the hyperfine structure of a single cesium atom is then described and numerically integrated to demonstrate the viability of implementing the scheme with a modern cavity QED system.

AI.tldr: Proposal for generating telecom-band quantum-correlated light from a single multilevel atom using two-photon transitions and cavity coupling.
AI.motivation: To create a source of quantum-correlated light in the telecom band (important for quantum communication) using a single atom, which can provide antibunched photon statistics characteristic of atomic sources.
AI.method: Use two lasers to drive a two-photon transition to an atomic excited state that emits telecom-band photons. Couple a cavity mode to the telecom transition to enhance emission rate while maintaining antibunched statistics. Explore adding a second independent cavity mode to increase emission rate and create quantum correlations between modes. Model hyperfine structure of cesium atom for numerical demonstration.
AI.result: The scheme shows that cavity coupling can enhance telecom emission rate while preserving antibunched counting statistics. Adding a second cavity mode further increases emission rate and introduces quantum correlations between cavity modes. Numerical integration with cesium atom model demonstrates viability for modern cavity QED systems.
AI.conclusion: The proposed scheme provides a viable approach for generating quantum-correlated telecom-band light from single atoms using two-photon transitions and cavity QED techniques, with potential applications in quantum communication.

title: Are Bell's conditions for local realism general enough?
summary: Bell conditions for local realism are critically revisited. In particular for optical experiments I criticize Bell's proposed response of detectors to signals as extremely idealized. More physical conditions are proposed, whence a realistic local model of an optical experiment is possible which violates the Clauser-Horne (Bell) inequality. The possibility rests on the existence of a coincidence-time loophole in the experiments.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques Bell's theorem assumptions in optical experiments, proposing more physical detector response conditions that enable a local realistic model violating the Clauser-Horne inequality through a coincidence-time loophole.
AI.motivation: To critically re-examine Bell conditions for local realism in optical experiments, challenging Bell's idealized assumptions about detector response to signals as unrealistic for actual experimental setups.
AI.method: Proposes more physically realistic conditions for detector response in optical experiments, identifies a coincidence-time loophole, and develops a local realistic model that can violate the Clauser-Horne (Bell) inequality under these revised conditions.
AI.result: Demonstrates that a realistic local model of optical experiments is possible that violates the Clauser-Horne inequality, challenging the standard interpretation that Bell inequality violations necessarily disprove local realism in quantum optics experiments.
AI.conclusion: Bell's theorem conclusions about local realism in optical experiments may be premature due to idealized assumptions about detector response; the existence of a coincidence-time loophole allows for local realistic explanations of experimental results.

title: Dynamics of states of infinite quantum systems as a cornerstone of the second law of thermodynamics
summary: We improve on our version of the second law of thermodynamics as a deterministic theorem for quantum spin systems in two basic aspects. The first concerns the general statement of the second law: spontaneous changes in an adiabatically closed system will always be in the direction of increasing mean entropy, which rises to a maximal value. Two specific examples concern the transition from pure to mixed states in two different universality classes of dynamics in one dimension, one being the exponential model, the other the Dyson model, the dynamics of the latter exhibiting strong graphical evidence of quantum chaos, as a consequence of the results of Albert and Kiessling on the Cloitre function.

AI.tldr: The paper improves the second law of thermodynamics as a deterministic theorem for quantum spin systems, showing spontaneous changes in adiabatically closed systems always increase mean entropy to a maximum, with examples of pure-to-mixed state transitions in 1D exponential and Dyson models.
AI.motivation: To strengthen the second law of thermodynamics as a rigorous deterministic theorem for quantum spin systems, addressing limitations in previous formulations and providing concrete examples of entropy increase in specific dynamical models.
AI.method: Develops an improved mathematical formulation of the second law for quantum spin systems, then applies it to analyze pure-to-mixed state transitions in two 1D universality classes: the exponential model and the Dyson model, with the latter exhibiting quantum chaos properties based on Albert and Kiessling's results on the Cloitre function.
AI.result: Establishes that spontaneous changes in adiabatically closed quantum spin systems always increase mean entropy to a maximal value, with specific demonstrations in both exponential and Dyson models, where the Dyson model shows strong evidence of quantum chaos.
AI.conclusion: The second law of thermodynamics can be formulated as a rigorous deterministic theorem for quantum spin systems, with entropy increase demonstrated in concrete 1D models including those exhibiting quantum chaos behavior.

title: Fast magic state preparation by gauging higher-form transversal gates in parallel
summary: Magic states are a foundational resource for universal quantum computation. To survive in a realistic noisy environment, magic states must be prepared fault-tolerantly and protected by a quantum error-correcting code. The recent discovery of highly efficient quantum low-density parity-check codes, together with efficient logic gates, lays the groundwork for low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computation. This motivates the search for fast and parallel protocols for logical magic state preparation to enable universal quantum computation. Here, we introduce a fast code surgery procedure that performs a fault-tolerant measurement of many transversal logic gates in parallel. This is achieved by performing a generalized gauging measurement on a quantum code that supports a higher-form transversal gate. The time overhead of our procedure is constant, and the qubit overhead is linear. The procedure inherits fault-tolerance properties from the base code and the structure of the higher-form transversal gate. When applied to codes that support higher-form Clifford gates our procedure achieves fast and fault-tolerant preparation of many magic states in parallel. This motivates the search for good quantum low-density parity-check codes that support higher-form Clifford gates.

AI.tldr: Fast, fault-tolerant parallel magic state preparation using code surgery and higher-form transversal gates in quantum LDPC codes.
AI.motivation: Magic states enable universal quantum computation but require fault-tolerant preparation. Recent advances in quantum LDPC codes with efficient logic gates motivate the search for fast, parallel protocols for logical magic state preparation to reduce overhead in fault-tolerant quantum computation.
AI.method: Introduces a fast code surgery procedure that performs fault-tolerant measurement of many transversal logic gates in parallel. This is achieved through generalized gauging measurements on quantum codes that support higher-form transversal gates. The procedure inherits fault-tolerance from the base code and the structure of the higher-form transversal gate.
AI.result: The procedure achieves constant time overhead and linear qubit overhead. When applied to codes supporting higher-form Clifford gates, it enables fast, fault-tolerant preparation of many magic states in parallel.
AI.conclusion: The approach motivates the search for good quantum LDPC codes that support higher-form Clifford gates, which would enable efficient, low-overhead universal quantum computation through parallel magic state preparation.

title: High-resolution tunable frequency beamsplitter enabled by an integrated silicon pulse shaper
summary: We demonstrate high-fidelity, tunable, and ultrafine-resolution on-chip frequency beamsplitters using a quantum frequency processor based on an integrated pulse shaper with six spectral channels. Near-ideal Hadamard gate performance is achieved, with fidelity F > 0.9995 and modified success probability P > 0.9621 maintained across frequency spacings from 2-5 GHz and down to as few as four spectral pulse shaper channels. The system's support of frequency spacings as narrow as 2 GHz significantly surpasses prior bulk demonstrations and enables arbitrary splitting ratios via spectral phase or modulation index control. These results establish a scalable and resource-efficient platform for integrated frequency-bin quantum photonics, opening new directions in quantum information processing, including densely parallel single-qubit operations and multidimensional gate implementations.

AI.tldr: High-fidelity on-chip frequency beamsplitters using quantum frequency processor with integrated pulse shaper achieve near-ideal Hadamard gate performance across 2-5 GHz frequency spacings.
AI.motivation: To develop scalable, resource-efficient integrated frequency-bin quantum photonics platforms that surpass prior bulk demonstrations and enable densely parallel quantum operations.
AI.method: Used quantum frequency processor based on integrated pulse shaper with six spectral channels, achieving tunable frequency beamsplitters via spectral phase or modulation index control.
AI.result: Achieved fidelity F > 0.9995 and modified success probability P > 0.9621 across frequency spacings from 2-5 GHz, supporting spacings as narrow as 2 GHz with as few as four spectral channels.
AI.conclusion: Establishes scalable platform for integrated frequency-bin quantum photonics enabling arbitrary splitting ratios and opening new directions in quantum information processing.

title: Dicke superposition probes for noise-resilient Heisenberg and super-Heisenberg Metrology
summary: Phase sensing with entangled multiqubit states in the presence of noise is a central theme of modern quantum metrology. The present work investigates Dicke state superposition probes for quantum phase sensing under parameter encoding generated by one- and two-body interaction Hamiltonians. A class of N-qubit Dicke superposition states that exhibit near-Heisenberg scaling, of the quantum Fisher information, while maintaining significantly enhanced robustness to dephasing noise compared to GHZ, W-superposition, and balanced Dicke states, under unitary encodings generated by one-body interaction Hamiltonians are identified. For two-body interactions, Dicke superposition probes optimizing the quantum Fisher information are identified, and their performance under phase-damping, amplitude-damping, and global depolarizing noise is explored. Within this family, certain Dicke superpositions are found to combine super-Heisenberg scaling with improved resilience to phase damping relative to Fisher information optimal probes. These results establish tailored near-optimal Dicke-state superposition probes as versatile and noise-resilient resources for Heisenberg and super-Heisenberg quantum phase sensing governed by one- and two-body interactions.

AI.tldr: Dicke state superposition probes achieve near-Heisenberg/super-Heisenberg scaling with enhanced noise resilience for quantum phase sensing under one- and two-body interactions.
AI.motivation: Phase sensing with entangled multiqubit states in noisy environments is crucial for quantum metrology, requiring probes that combine high precision (Heisenberg scaling) with noise resilience.
AI.method: Investigates Dicke state superposition probes for quantum phase sensing under parameter encoding generated by one- and two-body interaction Hamiltonians. Analyzes quantum Fisher information scaling and noise resilience under dephasing, phase-damping, amplitude-damping, and global depolarizing noise.
AI.result: Identified N-qubit Dicke superposition states exhibiting near-Heisenberg scaling with significantly enhanced robustness to dephasing noise compared to GHZ, W-superposition, and balanced Dicke states for one-body interactions. For two-body interactions, found Dicke superpositions that combine super-Heisenberg scaling with improved resilience to phase damping relative to Fisher information optimal probes.
AI.conclusion: Tailored near-optimal Dicke-state superposition probes serve as versatile and noise-resilient resources for Heisenberg and super-Heisenberg quantum phase sensing governed by one- and two-body interactions.

title: Scalable Memory Sharing in Photonic Quantum Memristors for Reservoir Computing
summary: Although photons are robust, room-temperature carriers well suited to quantum machine learning, the absence of photon-photon interactions hinder the realization of memory functionalities that are critical for capturing long-range context. Recently, measurement-based implementations of photonic quantum memristors (PQMRs) have enabled tunable non-Markovian responses. However, their memory remains confined to local elements, in contrast to biological or artificial networks where memory is shared across the system. Here, we propose a scalable PQMR network that enables measurement-based memory sharing. Each memristive node updates its internal state using the history of its own and neighbouring quantum states, thereby realizing distributed memory. By modelling each node as a photonic quantum memtransistor, we demonstrate pronounced enhancements in both classical and quantum hysteresis at the device level, as well as enhanced network-level quantum hysteresis. Implemented as a quantum reservoir, the architecture achieves improved Fashion-MNIST classification accuracy and confidence via increased data separability. Our approach paves the way toward high-capacity quantum machine learning using memristive devices compatible with linear-optical quantum computing.

AI.tldr: Scalable photonic quantum memristor network enables measurement-based memory sharing across nodes, enhancing quantum hysteresis and improving quantum reservoir computing performance for image classification.
AI.motivation: Photons are robust quantum carriers for machine learning but lack photon-photon interactions needed for memory functionalities. Existing photonic quantum memristors have memory confined to local elements, unlike biological/artificial networks where memory is shared across the system.
AI.method: Propose scalable photonic quantum memristor network with measurement-based memory sharing. Each memristive node updates internal state using history of its own and neighboring quantum states, creating distributed memory. Model nodes as photonic quantum memtransistors.
AI.result: Demonstrate pronounced enhancements in classical and quantum hysteresis at device level, and enhanced network-level quantum hysteresis. As quantum reservoir, achieves improved Fashion-MNIST classification accuracy and confidence via increased data separability.
AI.conclusion: Approach enables high-capacity quantum machine learning using memristive devices compatible with linear-optical quantum computing, paving way for distributed memory in photonic quantum systems.

title: Margin-Based Generalisation Bounds for Quantum Kernel Methods under Local Depolarising Noise
summary: Generalisation refers to the ability of a machine learning (ML) model to successfully apply patterns learned from training data to new, unseen data. Quantum devices in the current Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era are inherently affected by noise, which degrades generalisation performance. In this work, we derive upper and lower margin-based generalisation bounds for Quantum Kernel-Assisted Support Vector Machines (QSVMs) under local depolarising noise. These theoretical bounds characterise noise-induced margin decay and are validated via numerical simulations across multiple datasets, as well as experiments on real quantum hardware. We further justify the focus on margin-based measures by empirically establishing margins as a reliable indicator of generalisation performance for QSVMs. Additionally, we motivate the study of local depolarising noise by presenting empirical evidence demonstrating that the commonly used global depolarising noise model is overly optimistic and fails to accurately capture the degradation of generalisation performance observed in the NISQ era.

AI.tldr: Derived theoretical margin-based generalization bounds for Quantum Kernel-Assisted SVMs under local depolarizing noise, validated through simulations and real hardware experiments, showing margins as reliable generalization indicators and demonstrating global depolarizing noise is overly optimistic.
AI.motivation: Quantum devices in the NISQ era suffer from noise that degrades generalization performance, but existing noise models (like global depolarizing) are overly optimistic and fail to accurately capture generalization degradation in real quantum hardware.
AI.method: Derived upper and lower margin-based generalization bounds for QSVMs under local depolarizing noise, validated through numerical simulations across multiple datasets and experiments on real quantum hardware, while empirically establishing margins as reliable generalization indicators.
AI.result: Theoretical bounds characterize noise-induced margin decay, validated by simulations and hardware experiments; margins are empirically established as reliable generalization indicators; global depolarizing noise is shown to be overly optimistic compared to local depolarizing noise.
AI.conclusion: Local depolarizing noise provides more accurate modeling of generalization degradation in NISQ-era quantum devices than global depolarizing noise, and margin-based measures are reliable indicators of generalization performance for QSVMs.

title: TopoLS: Lattice Surgery Compilation via Topological Program Transformations
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing with surface codes can be achieved by compiling logical circuits into lattice-surgery instructions. To minimize space-time volume, we present TopoLS, a topological compiler that combines ZX-diagram optimizations with Monte Carlo tree search guided by different operation placements and topology-aware circuit partitioning. Our approach enables scalable exploration of lattice surgery structures and consistently reduces resource overhead. Evaluations of various benchmark algorithms across multiple architectures show that TopoLS achieves an average 33% reduction in space-time volume over prior heuristic-based compilers, while maintaining linear compilation time scaling. Compared to the SAT-solver-based compiler, which provides optimal results only for small circuits before becoming intractable, TopoLS offers an effective and scalable solution for lattice-surgery compilation.

AI.tldr: TopoLS is a topological compiler for fault-tolerant quantum computing that reduces space-time volume by 33% over prior heuristic methods through ZX-diagram optimizations and Monte Carlo tree search with topology-aware circuit partitioning.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing with surface codes requires compiling logical circuits into lattice-surgery instructions, and there's a need to minimize space-time volume while maintaining scalability, as existing SAT-solver-based approaches become intractable for large circuits.
AI.method: TopoLS combines ZX-diagram optimizations with Monte Carlo tree search guided by different operation placements and topology-aware circuit partitioning, enabling scalable exploration of lattice surgery structures.
AI.result: TopoLS achieves an average 33% reduction in space-time volume over prior heuristic-based compilers while maintaining linear compilation time scaling, offering an effective and scalable solution compared to SAT-solver-based approaches that become intractable for larger circuits.
AI.conclusion: TopoLS provides a scalable and effective topological compiler for lattice-surgery compilation that significantly reduces resource overhead while maintaining computational efficiency, addressing the limitations of both heuristic and optimal compilation approaches.

title: Free encoding capacity: A universal unit for quantum resources
comment: 4.5 pages + 4.5 pages, 4 Figs. Comments are welcome
summary: A perfect d-dimensional quantum channel can convey log d-bits of classical information by encoding messages in d-orthogonal quantum states.
